verdictReason: Killed. Demand is real (code-mandated cycles; a listed NorCal firm shows ~600 repeat clients, $375K revenue, $90K cash flow) but a stranger has no structural edge: the IKECA exam is open ($750 non-member, no stated prerequisite), photo records are commodity software, incumbents and a 135-unit franchise hold the accounts, and no source shows a newcomer winning a first restaurant. Year 1: +$4.9K only at 3 new accounts/month with an already-owned van; pessimistic -$16.2K; buying a van ($10-30K) breaks the $10K cap.

answers.question: What do certification, insurance and equipment cost a new firm (open cost question)?
answers.answer: Certification: IKECA lets a candidate sit the CECS exam after agreeing to the Code of Conduct (no experience prerequisite stated); the handbook fee table shows $750 for an individual non-member (read through a page summary; handbook version 7.20 may be old). IKECA company membership is optional: $995/yr dues + $250 application (introductory tier $575 + $100) and a $2M liability/completed-operations policy. Insurance (GL + workers comp): $3,000-$6,000/yr from a low-reliability guide. Equipment: hot-water pressure washer, ladders, safety gear roughly $5,000 on that guide; a used work van/pickup $10,000-$30,000. Whole-business estimates range from "$5,000 or even lower" to $10,000-$50,000. So $9K only closes if the stranger already owns a suitable vehicle and pays insurance monthly; otherwise it exceeds the cap.

answers.question: Is certification a barrier that protects a new entrant, or at least a cheap ticket anyone can get?
answers.answer: It is a cheap, open ticket, not an edge. IKECA requires no stated prerequisite to sit the exam, and a Nevada rule shows the state-licence route is an exam (>=75%) plus an employer letter, with uncertified helpers allowed under a certified supervisor on site. Incumbents hold the same credentials, so it excludes only uncertified amateurs, not rivals. Which states/AHJs accept which credentials was verified for Nevada only.

answers.question: Can a stranger win accounts from incumbents (open channel question)?
answers.answer: No public source shows it. The one first-hand source is a new kitchen-exhaust firm asking how to get a first restaurant to say yes; the only reply is untested walk-in advice, with no results reported. Guides say clients "will likely come from direct outreach". A listed incumbent claims ~600 clients with repeat cycles amid "numerous regional and national players", and Hoodz has 135 units (franchise cost $184K-$232K, out of budget). Generic commercial-cleaning leads cost $50-$150 each (not hood-specific). Assumed 3 wins/month is unevidenced.

answers.question: Is the digital service certificate with before/after photos an exclusive or compounding edge?
answers.answer: No. Software vendors already sell timestamped pre/post-photo service records to hotels and operators, and fire-marshal report-submission platforms exist for contractors (the Arlington page covers suppression systems, not hood cleaning, so this is only partial evidence). Any rival can adopt such tools; the record-holding secondary edge claimed earlier is therefore replicable and hands over with the account.

answers.question: What do first-365-day economics look like bottom-up for the reference entrant?
answers.answer: Baseline (assumption-heavy): 3 new accounts/month from month 3, 2 visits/account/year, $600/visit: 42 visits, revenue $25,200, cost $20,260 (fixed $14,800 + $130/visit), profit +$4,940 with owner unpaid and no vehicle purchase. Break-even is about 32 visits. Pessimistic (price x0.8, volume x0.5, cost x1.5): 21 visits, revenue $10,080, cost $26,295, profit -$16,215. Price evidence spans ~$360/visit (supplier hourly-rate average, 2018) to $900 (guide average); a listed mature firm implies about $625 revenue per client per year ($375,000 / ~600), well below the 2-visits x $600 assumed per account.

answers.question: Are there free/cheap/DIY alternatives or adjacent substitutes not previously listed?
answers.answer: Newly found: grease-filter exchange services (cover filters only, price not published, performed alongside vent cleaning), compliance software for tracking and photo records (price not published), per-hour price anchors ($102.96/h two-man crew, 2018; $900 average job), and franchise networks (Hoodz). None is a free full substitute for certified duct cleaning, so the wedge is not displaced by a free tool, but several partly cover the record-keeping angle.

killReasons.reason: No structural edge: the IKECA exam needs only agreement to a code of conduct, the Nevada route is an exam plus employer letter, incumbents and franchises hold the same credentials, and timestamped photo records are sold as off-the-shelf software, so neither certification nor the digital certificate is exclusive or compounding.

First-customer channel unevidenced against entrenched incumbents: the only first-hand source is a new firm asking how to get a first restaurant, with untested advice; an incumbent lists ~600 repeat clients and numerous regional and national rivals; paid leads cost $50-$150 each and a franchise channel costs $184K+.

Capital and pessimistic economics: a bought work van is $10,000-$30,000 and whole-business estimates run $10,000-$50,000 (two sources), against a $10K cap; at price x0.8, volume x0.5, cost x1.5 year 1 loses about $16K, and break-even needs about 32 visits at baseline. Inputs are assumptions, but the structure is unfavourable.
Licensing is a patchwork: Nevada requires a State Fire Marshal licence and exam to clean Type 1 grease ducts plus a city/county business licence; other states and AHJs were not verified.

assumptions: ASSUMPTION: months 1-2 are setup (certification, insurance, equipment, quoting); accounts are won from month 3 to month 12; first cleaning happens at signing; later visits at 12/visits-per-year month intervals; first revenue about day 60-90.

ASSUMPTION: baseline 3 new recurring accounts per month and an average of 2 visits per account per year (LOC3-E3 says most hoods are quarterly, but a listed mature firm implies about $625 revenue per client per year, LOC-3-D13 figures as read via summary).
ASSUMPTION: $600 revenue per visit (anchored on LOC3-E1 starting price $475; LOC-3-D9 average job $900; LOC-3-D12 implies about $360 for 3.5 h at $102.96/h).

ASSUMPTION: variable cost $130 per visit = one paid helper 3.5 h x $20/h ($70) + $60 consumables, fuel and disposal; owner works the second crew seat unpaid (3.5 h per visit comes from an earlier page summary, not re-verified).

ASSUMPTION: fixed year-1 cost $14,800 = equipment $5,000 (hot-water pressure washer about $3,000, ladders and safety $1,500, chemicals and tools $500) + certification and training $1,500 ($750 CECS non-member fee per LOC-3-D1 plus $750 assumed study/training) + insurance $4,500 (midpoint of LOC-3-D7) + marketing $3,000 (about 20-60 leads at LOC-3-D17 $50-$150) + licences, LLC, software and accounting $800.
ASSUMPTION: the entrant already owns a suitable pickup or van with ladder rack; if not, add $10,000-$30,000 (LOC-3-D8) and the $10K cap is breached.
Peak cash need before first revenue is about $11,000-$12,000 if insurance is paid annually and marketing is front-loaded; it fits $10K only with monthly insurance and staged marketing.

Pessimistic case applies price x0.8 ($480), volume x0.5 (1.5 accounts/month, 21 visits) and cost x1.5 to all fixed and variable costs: revenue $10,080, cost $26,295, profit -$16,215. Baseline profit +$4,940 is before any owner wage (about 147 crew hours plus sales and admin).

Owner-hours and mature-business upside (listing: $375,000 revenue, $90,000 cash flow, 3 full-time staff, about 600 clients, broker asking claims) are not reachable within the first 365 days from a standing start.

legalNotes: LOC-3-D4: Nevada requires a State Fire Marshal licence (exam, score >= 75%, employer letter, NFPA 96 knowledge) to service and clean Type 1 exhaust grease ducts, plus a city or county business licence; uncertified employees may assist only under direct on-site supervision (LOC-3-D5). Other states and AHJs differ and were not verified.

IKECA certification and membership are private credentials, not statutes; they matter because many AHJs, insurers and restaurant buyers ask for them (LOC3-E4, earlier evidence). Membership requires a $2M liability and completed-operations policy (LOC-3-D3).
Fire-suppression system inspection and recharge is a separate licensed activity and is outside this wedge (LOC3-E10).
No ToS barrier to the business itself; this research read only public pages without logins or contact.
unverified: All page text was read through WebFetch's summarizing model; quotes are copied from what it returned and were not diffed against raw page source. Table values (for example the $750 non-member CECS fee) were rendered by the summarizer, not quoted as sentences.

The IKECA CECS handbook fetched is version 7.20 (date unknown, possibly 2020); the newer 1.26 handbook could not be fetched, so current fees and any new experience prerequisite are unconfirmed. IKECA training-course cost was not found.
Insurance premium, van, washer and equipment prices come from a low-reliability unattributed guide (nikonomics-tools) and two generic blogs; no insurer quote or equipment-vendor price was read.
Whether AHJs in most states accept non-IKECA credentials, or require a state licence, was confirmed only for Nevada; the Boston fire-prevention page failed to load.

No hood-specific customer-acquisition cost, close rate, contract length, switching rate or churn was found; the $50-$150 lead figure is for generic commercial cleaning. Whether a newcomer can reach 3 accounts per month is the decisive unknown and public pages did not settle it.
The BizBuySell listing figures ($399,000 ask, $375,000 revenue, $90,000 cash flow, about 600 clients) are an unaudited broker claim read via summary; numbers are not in the quoted text.

HoodMart $102.96/hour is from 2018 and may be stale; the per-visit hours (3-4 h) come from earlier work and were not re-verified. Brycer fee schedule was an unreadable image; compliance-software and filter-exchange prices are not published.
nextStep: Drop it unless a public source shows unaffiliated new firms reaching about 20 recurring restaurant accounts within 12 months of starting.
